venues.d: A low, calm grande dame beside St Patrick's Cathedral and Fitzroy Gardens — the surest luxury in the city.
The top seventeen floors of Australia's tallest hotel — the city and Port Phillip Bay laid out beneath the glass.
The riverside landmark of Melbourne luxury — grand suites, a serious spa and the city's marquee dining under one roof.
Melbourne's original grand hotel on the smart end of Collins Street — a polished city house for three decades.
A gracious riverside grande dame on Southbank — afternoon tea, a celebrated spa and the city skyline across the Yarra.
An all-suite boutique house in leafy South Yarra — hushed, residential and quietly indulgent.
A biophilic, greenery-draped tower on the river — sustainable luxury with a rooftop pool over the city.
A design-led tower above the theatre district — warm, contemporary rooms and a rooftop bar over the city.
Twelve suites facing the Royal Botanic Gardens — a private residence in all but name.
A long-loved all-suite hotel in the heart of chic South Yarra — the address for Chapel Street and the boutiques.
Australia's grand Victorian hotel, opposite Parliament since 1883 — old-world grandeur and a legendary afternoon tea.
A bold, laneway-inspired design tower on Flinders Lane — colour, energy and a buzzing bar scene.
A sleek, art-filled hotel tucked into a heritage Collins Street arcade — central, contemporary and well-run.
A playful, fashion-forward design hotel with one of the city's liveliest rooftop bars.
A bright, art-splashed design hotel on Chapel Street — colour, fun and generous inclusions.
Native Australian produce, high above the city on the 55th floor of the Rialto — the definitive Melbourne occasion.
A quiet suburban room cooking at the very top of the national game — intimate, precise, deeply personal.
Melbourne's temple of sushi — a serene omakase counter of great purity, the finest in the country.
Ben Shewry's storytelling through native Australian ingredients — one of the most influential kitchens on earth.
The grand dame of Cantonese dining in Chinatown since 1975 — Peking duck and impeccable service, named the city's best.
Andrew McConnell's glamorous 1920s-style dining room and bar — oysters, wood-grill and a room that never disappoints.
Andrew McConnell's flagship — a handsome, grown-up Fitzroy room of confident modern cooking.
Khanh Nguyen's fire-and-smoke cooking — Southeast-Asian roots met with the wood grill, bold and precise.
A hidden basement kaiseki counter of great refinement — a serene, ceremonial Japanese seasonal menu.
A six-seat mezzanine counter marrying Japanese technique and Australian produce — intimate and exacting.
Grand French dining in a restored heritage banking chamber — the city's most opulent room for classic cooking.
Ronnie Di Stasio's art-filled Italian temple — precise, uncompromising, and unmistakably Melbourne.
Peter Gunn's inventive, personality-driven tasting menu — one of the inner-north's most exciting kitchens.
Victor Liong's modern Chinese in a laneway room — the crispy eel and considered cooking made its name.
Japanese technique meets French finesse — a refined, quietly ambitious Carlton degustation.
A tiny, produce-obsessed west-side room cooking a precise modern tasting menu well above its postcode.
A serene, considered Japanese room — seasonal and delicate, one of the city's most rewarding tables.
A glamorous, old-school Italian room of tableside theatre and generous cooking — a return to grand hospitality.
Modern Southeast-Asian cooking in a laneway room — the roti and native-ingredient plates are the city's most creative.
An intimate, exacting Japanese counter in the west — quietly one of Melbourne's finest kitchens.
Thi Le's Viet-Kieu cooking — Australian and Vietnamese in one voice, from the city's Chef of the Year.
An assured new arrival that arrived fully formed — the city's New Restaurant of the Year.
A grand upstairs Italian dining room, muralled and gilded, that has anchored Bourke Street for generations.
Andrew McConnell's buzzing Asian diner — the lobster roll and dumplings pack it every night.
A classic Parisian bistro that has never gone out of style — steak frites, a great cellar and proper bustle.
Regional Indian cooking with real conviction — a newcomer that earned its hat on the food alone.
A tiny, always-packed pasta bar — house-made pasta done with real finesse, and a cult following.
The Thai-street-food juggernaut that changed how Melbourne eats out — loud, generous and endlessly fun.
Andrew McConnell's all-day Flinders Lane room — the slow-roast lamb shoulder is a Melbourne rite.
Migrant-melting-pot cooking with heart and swagger — one of the most exciting casual rooms in the north.
Andrew McConnell's wine bar next to Cutler & Co. — small plates, natural wine and Fitzroy warmth.
A long-loved Iberian tapas bar — sherry, cured meats and a devoted following for two decades.

Melbourne's angular civic heart, facing Flinders Street Station across the river — a good first anchor for orienting the city, with the Ian Potter Centre and ACMI opening off the plaza. A private guide can start you here and walk you into the laneways within minutes.

The most famous of Melbourne's graffiti bluestone lanes, a wall-to-wall canvas that changes weekly and runs off Flinders Lane opposite Fed Square. Even a short walk-through gives the family the city's counter-culture in ten minutes; nearby Rutledge Lane extends it.

A narrow cobbled lane packed with awning-shaded cafe tables — the postcard of Melbourne's coffee culture. Order a flat white standing at a hole-in-the-wall roaster and watch the city's obsession up close.

Two exquisitely preserved Victorian-era shopping arcades: the Block with its mosaic-tiled floor and the historic Hopetoun Tea Rooms, and Royal Arcade with its Gog and Magog figures. Genteel, unhurried and a lovely stop between laneways for tea and chocolate.

Australia's oldest and most-visited public gallery, whose St Kilda Road building holds the international collection behind a famous water-wall entrance. The blockbuster summer exhibitions and the stained-glass Great Hall ceiling are worth timed tickets; entry to the permanent collection is free.

The Fed Square site of the NGV devoted entirely to Australian art, including the country's most significant collection of Indigenous art. A shorter, focused visit that pairs naturally with Federation Square for a multi-generation morning.

Thirty-eight hectares of lakes, lawns and rare plantings sweeping down toward the river — Melbourne's green lungs and an easy, buggy-friendly wander for elders and children alike. Take the Aboriginal Heritage Walk or an Punt Road picnic; the Tan track circles it.

Melbourne's grand war memorial on a rise above the Botanic Gardens, its ceremonial forecourt and city views making it one of the CBD's most dignified vantage points. Climb to the balcony for the sightline straight down Swanston Street to the city.

A sprawling 19th-century open-air market — delis, produce, seafood and the Winter/Summer Night Markets — and the best single place to graze the city's food cultures in one visit. A guided Ultimate Foodie tour lets the family taste widely without the crush.

The spiritual home of Australian sport and one of the world's great stadiums, holding 100,000 for AFL and cricket. A behind-the-scenes tour of the members' rooms and the arena thrills any sports-loving traveller; a Boxing Day Test or an AFL final is a bucket-list day.

Inside the MCG, an immersive museum of Australian sport — cricket, AFL, the Olympics and the Australian Open — with interactive galleries the children will not want to leave. Combine it with the stadium tour.

The Southern Hemisphere's highest public viewing platform, on the 88th floor at 285m, with 360-degree views and 'The Edge' glass cube that slides out over the city. Best at dusk to catch daylight then the lit skyline; the recently rebranded Eureka Skydeck.

One of the world's most beautiful reading rooms — the domed octagonal La Trobe Reading Room — free to enter and quietly spectacular from the upper galleries. A serene pause from the CBD, and home to the Ned Kelly armour.
Housed in the old Customs House, it tells the story of the peoples who built Melbourne — a resonant stop for Indian families, tracing the migration threads that make the city so plural today.

Australia's first UNESCO-listed building, a soaring 1880 exhibition palace set in formal Victorian gardens beside Melbourne Museum. Time a dome-promenade tour; the gardens are a lovely picnic setting for elders and children.

A modern natural-history and cultural museum beside the Exhibition Building, with the Bunjilaka Aboriginal Cultural Centre, a living rainforest gallery and the beloved racehorse Phar Lap. Genuinely absorbing across three generations, and there is an IMAX alongside.

Melbourne's original bohemian quarter and still its most characterful — independent boutiques, record shops, wine bars and some of the city's best small dining. The neighbourhood to walk slowly with a coffee and let the family drift.

Once industrial, now the city's hottest strip — Smith Street runs from cult roasters to natural-wine bars and the rooftop of the old Foy & Gibson warehouses. A cool-hunter's afternoon for younger travellers.

venues.n: Brunswick — Sydney Road & Lygon Street north
venues.d: A multicultural strip of Middle Eastern grocers, live-music rooms and third-wave cafes, north of the centre and refreshingly un-touristed. Good for a driver to loop through for a taste of the real, everyday Melbourne.
The historic Italian quarter where Melbourne's espresso culture began, lined with trattorias and gelaterie. An easy, crowd-pleasing dinner street a short hop from the Exhibition Building and museum.

venues.n: St Kilda Pier & the little-penguin colony
venues.d: A newly rebuilt pier reaching into Port Phillip Bay, where around 1,400 wild little penguins come ashore at dusk on the breakwater — free to view from the boardwalk. A magical, gentle evening for children; go at sunset and keep torches off.

The 1912 amusement park behind its famous grinning Mr Moon face on the Esplanade, home to one of the world's oldest continually operating roller-coasters (the Scenic Railway). Nostalgic and photogenic; open weekends and holidays.

Melbourne's bayside promenade — palm-lined beach, Sunday art market, and the grand old Espy hotel — an easy seaside afternoon 15 minutes from the CBD. Cakes on Acland Street's continental-cake row are a ritual.

The riverside arts-and-dining precinct across from Flinders Street — Arts Centre spire, restaurants along the water, and the launch point for river cruises. A pleasant sundown stroll with the skyline reflected in the Yarra.

A relaxed way to read the city from the water — sightseeing cruises run upriver toward the gardens and downriver to Docklands and the port. Charter a private vessel for a multi-gen group; a slow, low-effort highlight for elders.

A modern waterfront quarter of marinas, waterside dining and public art west of the CBD, reached by the free City Circle tram. Calmer than the centre and good for a harbourside lunch; the Melbourne Star wheel here is undergoing a planned reopening.

Under its lattice spire, the city's flagship performing-arts complex — ballet, opera, theatre and the Melbourne Symphony at Hamer Hall. Worth a night out; the Sunday market of makers runs along its forecourt.

A 19th-century convent turned rambling arts precinct on the riverbank — galleries, artist studios, gardens and the excellent Lentil As Anything and Convent Bakery. Free to wander, deeply atmospheric, and next to Collingwood Children's Farm for the little ones.

A grand formal park on the CBD's edge, with elm avenues, a fairy tree and the transplanted stone cottage of Captain Cook's family, shipped brick-by-brick from England. A short, shaded green stop for elders between sights.

One of the oldest continuous Chinatowns in the Western world, its arches spanning Little Bourke Street, with the Chinese Museum tucked among the restaurants. The address for late dumplings and the setting of Flower Drum.

Melbourne's legendary Cantonese fine-diner, quietly running for over forty years on Market Lane — Peking duck, aromatic baked crab, and discreet, faultless service. The special-occasion dinner for a discerning family; book well ahead.

The buzzing, all-day Southeast Asian diner on Flinders Lane that has drawn queues since 2011 — hawker-style shared plates built for a table of many. Lively, generous and easy for a mixed group; the 'Feed Me' menu takes the decisions away.

Melbourne's landmark fine-dining room on the 55th floor of the Rialto, a native-ingredient degustation with the whole city at your feet. The city's dress-up dinner; request a window and let the sommelier lead.

Ben Shewry's celebrated suburban restaurant, long ranked among the world's best, serving a deeply personal tasting menu of native Australian ingredients. A pilgrimage table for serious food travellers; reservations open in advance and go fast.
The single best street to eat in Melbourne — a dense run of hatted restaurants and wine bars from Movida's tapas to Cumulus Inc. Let a concierge match the room to your group; walkable end to end.

Coffee is a genuine civic craft here — a private roaster-hopping morning through hole-in-the-wall bars and single-origin cafes reveals the culture better than any sight. Ask for a barista-led tasting; the flat white is the local benchmark.

An hour east, Victoria's premier cool-climate wine region — cellar doors from Domaine Chandon's French sparkling house to acclaimed Pinot and Chardonnay estates, with long lunches among the vines. Ideal as a chauffeured day; several estates cater beautifully to non-drinkers and families.

An hour east into fern-gullied mountain forest, riding the century-old Puffing Billy steam train with legs dangling from open carriages — pure delight for children and grandparents alike. Add the William Ricketts sanctuary and a Sassafras tea room.

A vast, living re-creation of a 1850s gold-rush town about 90 minutes west — costumed streets, gold panning, and a nightly sound-and-light show. Immersive and hands-on for multi-generation groups curious about how Victoria's wealth was made.

A grand 1870s Italianate mansion in formal gardens 30 minutes south-west, beside Shadowfax winery and the Werribee Open Range Zoo. A gentle, elegant half-day that combines heritage, wine and a safari-style drive for children.

The linked chain of parkland ringing the CBD — Kings Domain, Alexandra Gardens and the riverbank — makes for a long, level walk or a hired-bike loop past the Shrine and the rowing sheds. An easy way to see the city's famed green ring.

The year's first tennis Grand Slam, drawing the world to Melbourne Park each January — night sessions under lights at Rod Laver Arena are electric. Corporate suites and premium hospitality make it a marquee outing; book the season far ahead.

Formula 1 returns to the parkland circuit around Albert Park Lake each autumn, a fast street-style track minutes from the CBD. Trackside paddock and grandstand packages suit a group of enthusiasts; the city hums all weekend.

'The race that stops a nation' — the first Tuesday of November at Flemington, the centrepiece of a spring carnival of fashion, marquees and champagne. The Birdcage enclosure is the ticket for a memorable, dressed-up day.
A tiny 1850s bluestone gatehouse turned world-ranked bar — an English-pub soul, faultless drinks, and Guinness on draught.
A cult experimental bar of native-ingredient, terroir-driven drinks — hidden behind a food court, and worth the hunt.
Twelve seats, no standing, and some of the finest bartending in Australia — a purist's cocktail room.
A polished, grown-up cocktail-and-food room where the drinking and the eating are equally serious.
An intimate, expertly-run small bar — the country's best, honouring the craft without the ceremony.
A handsome, ambitious newcomer that arrived as the best new bar in the land — polished, warm and expertly poured.
Melbourne's beloved late-night institution — two decades of phenomenal cocktails and unshowy warmth.
A Paris-via-New York brasserie-bar open until the small hours — oysters, champagne and steak past midnight.
A hidden 1920s-style speakeasy of theatrical cocktails and a serious whisky room — the drama done properly.
A European rooftop terrace over Parliament and St Patrick's — cigars, cognac and old-world glamour.

venues.a: CBD (Rialto, Level 55, at Vue de Monde)
venues.d: A glamorous 55th-floor bar beside Vue de Monde — the whole city glittering beneath the glass.
